rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation changes `input_height = input.size(3)` to `input_height = input.size(2)`. With the fixed input shape [16, 32, 64, 64, 64], we have: input.size(2) = 64 (depth) and input.size(3) = 64 (height). Since depth == height == 64, both original and mutated code compute input_height = 64. The mutation produces identical behavior regardless of tensor values.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation swaps the dimension index used to read input_height (from index 3 to index 2). However, the fixed input specification requires shape [16, 32, 64, 64, 64], where the depth dimension (index 2) equals 64 and the height dimension (index 3) also equals 64. Since these dimensions are identical, the mutated code computes the exact same input_height value (64) as the original code. This makes all downstream calculations—output_height computation, ih_end clamping, depth_offset and height_offset indexing—produce bit-identical results. No value-level variation can expose this bug because the equality depth==height is a shape property, not a value property.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. To kill it would require an input tensor where depth ≠ height (e.g., shape [16, 32, 32, 64, 64]), which violates the contract that shapes never change. Since the fixed shape has depth=height=64, the mutation is semantically equivalent.
rounds.recommendations: When designing mutation tests for GPU kernels with multi-dimensional inputs, use input shapes with distinct dimension sizes (e.g., [16, 32, 32, 48, 64] instead of [16, 32, 64, 64, 64]) to ensure dimension-index mutations like this one are detectable. Symmetric shapes create blind spots where dimension swaps go unnoticed.
